claims.text: The initial material is an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metallic substrate.
The as-deposited coating has native, uncontrolled surface oxidation.
A short treatment such as 10 minutes at 500°C under low oxygen partial pressure constitutes the proposed controlled pre-oxidation intervention.
The controlled pre-oxidation treatment will form a uniform, adherent oxide layer on FeNiCrCoCu.
The pre-formed layer will be a stable, thin mixed-metal oxide, potentially a spinel or related phase.
The engineered oxide will remain adherent under cyclic high-load wear.
The oxide layer will reduce direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding.
The oxide layer will limit rapid further oxidation of the underlying metallic coating.
The oxide layer will act as a lubricious and sacrificial barrier.
The lubricious oxide will minimize adhesive interactions at the sliding interface.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have significantly lower friction coefficients than untreated as-deposited coatings.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have significantly lower wear rates than untreated as-deposited coatings.
Post-test analysis will show persistence of the engineered oxide layer.
Post-test analysis will show reduced oxidation and spallation in the pre-oxidized coating.
The untreated baseline develops a non-optimized, uncontrolled oxide layer.
The oxide formed on the untreated baseline does not effectively protect against high-temperature wear.
The proposed hypothesis is scoped to wear testing from 600°C to 800°C under cyclic high-load conditions.
Applicability outside 600°C to 800°C or under extreme thermal cycling is uncertain.
